summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for DS1, E1, DS2 and E2 interfaces, which are standard telephone-style digital line types. It is a companion to documents for DS0, DS3/E3 and synchronous optical interfaces. It was replaced by RFC 4805.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone-style data lines have meters that show their health. This document defines the meters. It was replaced by RFC 4805.

questions: snmp management of t1 e1 interfaces
subtitle: Define SNMP objects to monitor health and manage T1, E1, and higher-speed telephone-style digital lines.

tldr.problem: DS1, E1, DS2, and E2 are standard digital line technologies used in telecommunications and ISP networks, but network operators need standardized ways to monitor and manage these interfaces via SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) with objects for monitoring error rates, performance metrics, alarm conditions, loopback status, and line configuration on DS1/E1/DS2/E2 interfaces. Network management stations can query routers and line equipment for performance data collected over 15-minute intervals.
tldr.outcome: Operators can manage DS1/E1 networks using standard SNMP tools instead of vendor-specific interfaces. Equipment from different vendors can all be monitored with the same management system. It was updated by RFC 4805 to reflect evolving requirements.

today: RFC 3895 defines the MIB for managing DS1/E1/DS2/E2 interfaces and is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 2495 and was itself superseded by RFC 4805 in October 2006, which added support for new framing modes and updated compliance statements.

sections.title: DS1 and E1 Lines
sections.content:
DS1, E1, DS2, and E2 are standardized digital line types used globally for telecommunications and data networking. DS1 (T1 in North America) carries 1.544 Mbps, E1 (in Europe) carries 2.048 Mbps, DS2 carries 6.312 Mbps, and E2 carries 8.448 Mbps. These lines use specific framing formats: DS1 uses D4 or Extended Superframe (ESF) framing, and E1 follows CCITT G.703/G.704 recommendations.

This MIB is a companion to related documents defining management objects for DS0 (individual 64 kbps channels), DS3/E3 (higher-speed lines), and SONET/SDH (optical lines). The focus is on objects that can be read from deployed equipment: performance counters, error indicators, alarm states, and configuration options like loopback mode and line coding.
sections.plainLanguage: T1 and E1 are the phone company's standard data pipes. This document says how to measure if they are healthy.

sections.title: Error Counters and Performance Metrics
sections.content:
The MIB collects performance data in 15-minute intervals, storing up to 96 intervals (24 hours). Performance metrics fall into several categories. Line Errored Seconds (LES) count seconds where one or more line coding violations (flipped bit patterns) are detected. Path Errored Seconds (ES) count seconds with path coding violations, loss of frame, controlled slips, or alarm indication signals—essentially any second where something goes wrong.

Severely Errored Seconds (SES) count seconds with 320 or more path coding violations (ESF), or any out-of-frame defect or AIS. Unavailable Seconds (UAS) count periods when the interface is unusable: either 10 or more consecutive SES or a complete failure condition. When UAS starts, other counters freeze; only UAS increments during unavailability.

Bursty Errored Seconds (BES) and Degraded Minutes refine the error picture: BES counts seconds with a moderate number of errors (between 1 and 320 violations), and Degraded Minutes count 60-second periods where the estimated error rate is worse than 1E-6 but better than 1E-3.
sections.plainLanguage: The meters count bad seconds, really bad seconds, seconds when the line is dead, and minutes where quality is poor but not terrible.

sections.title: Alarm Conditions and Failure Detection
sections.content:
In addition to error counters, the MIB tracks active alarm conditions. Loss of Signal (LOS) is declared when no pulses are detected for 175 ± 75 bit intervals; it clears when at least 12.5% pulse density is observed over that period. Loss of Frame (LOF) occurs when two or more framing errors are detected in 3 msec (ESF) or 0.75 msec (D4), indicating the receiver is out of sync with the frame boundaries.

Alarm Indication Signal (AIS) is the "all-ones" condition: every bit is set to 1, indicating that the far end is experiencing a fault and sending a distress signal. Far End Alarm (Yellow/Remote Alarm) is signaled by the remote equipment when it detects a failure. Out Of Frame (OOF) is a precursor to LOF, declared when the framing pattern shows errors but the receiver is still hunting for frame alignment.

The MIB also tracks loopback state: either the local management station or the remote end can request a loopback, which sends all received data back to the sender for testing. The MIB distinguishes between line loopback (loops at the interface), payload loopback (loops the data within the frame), and inward loopback (loops transmitted data back before transmission).
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, the line shows an alarm: no signal, out of frame, the far end is screaming for help, or it is looped back for testing.

sections.title: Configuration and Line Parameters
sections.content:
The MIB allows operators to configure several line parameters. Line type specifies the format: ESF or D4 for DS1, CRC or non-CRC variants for E1, and corresponding modes for DS2/E2. Line coding specifies how bits are encoded: AMI (Alternate Mark Inversion) for standard DS1, B8ZS (Binary 8-Zero Substitution) to prevent long strings of zeros, or HDB3 (High-Density Bipolar) for E1.

Loopback configuration lets operators select which loopback mode (if any) should be active. The MIB distinguishes between loopbacks requested by the local management station and those requested by the remote end. Signal mode indicates the current signal state: normal, testing, or others.

The MIB also maps DS1/E1 lines to higher-speed carriers: when a DS3 is channelized into multiple DS1s, the MIB tracks which DS1 occupies which channel slot and provides parent-child relationships via ifStackTable. Similarly, DS1 lines can be channelized into individual 64 kbps DS0 channels.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators can tell the line what format to use, how to encode bits, and whether to test it by looping data back.

sections.title: SNMP Integration and Usage
sections.content:
This MIB is compliant with SMIv2 (Structure of Management Information version 2) and integrates with the standard interfaces MIB (RFC 2863). Each DS1/E1 line appears as an entry in the ifTable with ifType ds1(18). Basic ifTable objects like ifSpeed (1.544 Mbps for DS1, 2.048 for E1, etc.), ifAdminStatus, and ifOperStatus apply. The dsx1 table extends ifTable with DS1-specific objects for performance metrics and configuration.

For proxy scenarios (where an SNMP agent on a router manages remote CSU or DSU equipment), the ifStackTable represents the relationship between the router's interface and the equipment's interface. The MIB notes that the deprecated dsx1IfIndex object is replaced by this modern ifStackTable approach.

Network management stations use SNMP GET operations to retrieve current performance counters and alarm states, and SET operations to configure loopback, line type, and other parameters. Traps (asynchronous notifications) can alert the management station when line status changes.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP agents on routers and line equipment expose these metrics and settings. A network management station reads the meters and can change settings.

items.label: Loss of Signal
items.desc: No pulses detected for 175±75 bit intervals; link is completely dead.

items.label: Loss of Frame
items.desc: Frame synchronization lost; receiver cannot find frame boundaries.

items.label: Alarm Indication Signal
items.desc: All-ones signal received; far end is sending distress signal.

items.label: Remote Alarm Indication
items.desc: Far end detected a failure and is alerting the near end.
